title: Board guest prompts:
title_short: Board guests · Three words for today
headline: Three Watsi board members stand in the hospital and say, in the moment, what Watsi is and what seeing it in person changed.
story: Tiffany sums up the day in three words: inspirational, heartwarming, and fun. Margaret calls Watsi clickable joy. Raj and Tiffany say what it is in plain words.
Seeing it in person: Margaret's pride is in the organization here caring for families and kids; Tiffany sees that surgery changes the whole family.

Loops: L1 “Three words for what?” opens at 0:00 and closes in Margaret's “clickable joy”. L2 “What happens when they see it in person?” closes in the button. Stakes: as Watsi grows, the human connection is what could be lost. Margaret says it never will, and Raj thanks the donors.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of the four board interviews (Watsi Colombia Oct 20 2026, Clínica Noel, Medellín): Margaret Cornelius Mincho7659, Raj Malik Mincho7660 and Mincho7661, Dr. Tiffany Mincho7719. Times are mm:ss.s in each file, from the word timings in output.json. Fixed by hand: Watsi (transcript: WOTC), Medellín, Clínica Noel, Colombia. Speaker labels in the transcript are often wrong; Sonam asks the questions from behind the lens.

--- Mincho7659.MP4 ---
[00:01.6] Okay, so can you introduce yourself so you can start with like your name, where you're coming from, and you can just say something like I'm a Watsi Board Chair, so just like a quick introduction. [do not use: interviewer set-up]
[00:16.9] Great. [do not use: interviewer set-up]
[00:17.9] So my name is Margaret Cornelius, I live right outside of Washington DC with my family, and I've been working with Watsi as a board member for over five years.
[00:27.9] I'm also currently the chair of the board, and it's a true privilege to be working alongside Watsi and all of the team and all of the board members.
[00:38.1] How would you describe Watsi in your own words? [do not use: interviewer question]
[00:42.2] So when I think of Watsi, I think of clickable joy for anyone who wants to try to get off the website without funding a patient, it's not possible.
[00:55.2] Even myself as a longtime supporter of Watsi and member of the Universal Fund, if I ever find myself on the Watsi website, I absolutely have to close out some of the patients and fully fund them, I can't get away from it.
[01:10.2] It's a real place where anybody can support anyone in the world for anything that they need.
[01:16.8] And I just think that the power of that funding model for healthcare is just tremendously impactful.
[01:24.2] How does it feel to see this working person today? [do not use: interviewer question]
[01:28.5] So, I feel a great deal of pride, and also, to a certain extent, I don't need to see anything.
[01:38.2] I already know how powerful Watsi is and how much work they do.
[01:42.5] And really, for me, it's not so much about Watsi today, it's about this amazing organization here in Medellín that is caring for so many families and so many kids and has been doing it for so long.
[01:56.5] And to just be able to be here is just such a privilege.
[02:00.7] I really can't put words to it.
[02:06.3] This is coming off the cuff right now, but what do you hope Watsi doesn't lose as it grows? [do not use: interviewer question]
[02:14.3] So, of course, as the chair of the board, I want to see nothing but Watsi growing.
[02:21.5] And I've been able to actually see Watsi grow since it started over 10 years ago.
[02:28.3] And I know that what Watsi has always kept as it has grown is its authenticity and its tremendous effort to make sure that the human part of Watsi is always front and center.
[02:43.5] In healthcare, you often hear people say things like patient-centered or patients are the center of everything we do, but I really think that Watsi lives this in everything it does.
[02:55.3] And no matter where you are or who you're talking to, you can always pull up a patient and know immediately how that person's life has been changed in the tiny way that Watsi is able to support.
[03:07.3] And I know that Watsi will never lose that human connection.
[03:11.3] Next, probably the last question, Margaret. [do not use: interviewer question]
[03:13.1] A little broad though, so if you don't mind. [do not use: interviewer question]
[03:15.3] It's okay. [do not use: interviewer question]
[03:16.3] But something that's been on our head is we are living through a very strange time in health and in philanthropy. [do not use: interviewer question]
[03:25.0] What do you feel when you see the world right now? [do not use: interviewer question]
[03:29.9] What do I feel when I see the world in terms of the health sector and global health? [do not use: interviewer question]
[03:36.3] So I guess because I do come from financing and health financing, there's never enough to pay for everything that we want people to have. [do not use: money talk]
[03:49.3] And organizations and models that allow us to get the most out of what we do have to patients as quickly as possible are what I believe the future will look like. [do not use: money talk]
[04:04.8] And interestingly enough, Watsi is a very simple premise, it's making sure that resources that are in one place can get to a very difficult place or a place that needs more resources.
[04:17.5] And Watsi does it in such an efficient, powerful way.
[04:21.7] I would love to see more of that kind of model where it doesn't really matter where you are or what country you live in or what healthcare you do or do not have access to.
[04:31.5] With technology and with information, and hopefully more Watsi in the world, we will see more patients get access to care in more places because we will simply be able to get them resources more quickly and more transparently.
[04:47.4] Probably the last thing I'd like to ask you, any message of gratitude you'd like to share? [do not use: interviewer question]
[04:52.4] Messages of gratitude?
[04:55.4] Oh, I mean, infinite.
[04:56.9] Every time I think about or am told about a donor through Mackinnon or through a story we hear from somewhere else, just understanding what motivates people to come to Watsi, to come back to Watsi.
[05:13.4] I hope that you'll stay.
[05:15.1] I hope that you'll continue to partner and contribute and give us feedback on what we can do better and how we can reach you and reach your family and reach your own community.
[05:26.4] But I just hope you continue to come back to whatever it is that brings you joy, which brings you to Watsi.
[05:32.9] We're just so grateful for everything you do.
[05:35.6] You're welcome. [do not use: chat after the take]
[05:40.8] That means so much. [do not use: chat after the take]
[05:42.6] My pleasure. [do not use: chat after the take]

[00:03.7] So let's start with you just introducing yourself so you can say your name, where you're coming from, and you can say what's your role. [do not use: interviewer set-up]
[00:17.4] Hi, my name is Raj Malik.
[00:19.5] I came from the United States, Columbus, Ohio.
[00:23.7] I've been a board member now for almost three years.
[00:28.9] How would you describe Watsi in your own words to a fan? [do not use: interviewer question]
[00:33.9] So I can start with at least first the mission.
[00:37.4] The mission is trying to bring healthcare to more people that are needing it around the world.
[00:43.1] And so through a real community aspect where you have a person that might live in another country that could see somebody else that needs an important medical procedure that they can actually help fund so that medical procedure gets done and the person that needs it can live a healthier, better life.
[01:02.9] That's sort of the mission.
[01:05.0] What it means for me and why I'm so excited by Watsi is, frankly, when you were here in Colombia now and the time that I've spent here on site has been just overwhelming to some extent.
[01:20.1] It's been incredible.
[01:21.7] The work that's done here, the care that it's done with, and the impact on people's lives, it's phenomenal just to see and to see the real tangible impact that someone who might come in here with great need for some medical care can get it done, can get through, be helped, and then ultimately be able to live a much healthier, better life.

--- Mincho7661.MP4 ---
[00:00.0] I know you talked a little bit about being here and seeing the world, but could you share a little more about how do you feel after seeing the world in action today? [do not use: interviewer question]
[00:13.2] So, today has been, we've seen patients, we've seen surgeries, we've met surgeons, we've met staff as well too.
[00:24.4] And most importantly, we've seen patients and families.
[00:28.4] And to see sort of the whole experience, to go from a patient that literally we're seeing in the waiting room, see us first and be a little surprised at who are these folks that are coming here, obviously on behalf of Watson.
[00:43.6] But to be able to see that patient, a little child, have tears in their eyes because they're scared.
[00:52.6] They have no idea.
[00:53.6] They're being pulled by their parents.
[00:55.4] They'll be alright.
[00:56.4] They're being reassured by a physician.
[00:59.6] But to walk in the shoes of a little child at 95, 6, 7, 8 years old, getting hopefully life-changing medical treatment is phenomenal.
[01:15.6] To actually be able to go into the operating room and actually see the surgeon in there operating, not just with one doctor, multiple doctors that are in there and the whole staff.
[01:30.6] And then at the end to be able to see the patient come out of there and in recovery, super powerful.
[01:39.6] And then obviously the parent, the mother, the father that's there that's worrying throughout the whole process of getting the care, seeing the actual procedure get done, and then seeing the smile on the face of that young patient is just incredible.
[02:00.6] After seeing the work here, what are you most excited for, what's it to figure out next? [do not use: interviewer question]
[02:07.4] I say this to Mackinnon and as a board member, I say it to the board a lot. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[02:12.4] I think it is our mission and it should be one of our missions too. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[02:18.8] This needs to be in every place. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[02:21.8] Watsi, Watsi-sponsored medical facilities needs to be in every place around the world for patients who need care. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[02:30.8] Because unfortunately, there's an unending number of patients around the world that need this care. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[02:38.3] And one thing we were just talking about today is there's a lot of folks, a lot of folks who just don't get that care, they don't have access. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[02:46.8] We literally heard about a person today who ended up taking a first abort to go get to a bus, to go get to a metro station, and then a train to be able to go. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]

[03:38.5] And we can all do something to change that. [do not use: saved for a standalone cut (02:07 to 03:38)]
[03:49.4] So India, from what I've seen, what I've heard, it's the very first medical clinic that has been set up there. [do not use: restart and crew talk]

[04:24.9] So India is in such need for medical infrastructure and medical care to be provided because there's, again, such a major need with such a large population.
[04:39.3] So the ability for Watsi to be able to go not just where it's at one point and to be able to go beyond that, it could be transformational for the Indian health care system.
[04:54.3] That's not something that's a model that has really been known and not accepted.
[04:59.3] So I hope for Watsi to be able to actually have, for the first time, be able to go there, be aligned with an incredibly, incredibly well-known physician, and be able to hopefully spread the Watsi brand throughout.
[05:18.3] Last question. [do not use: interviewer question]
[05:20.3] We are approaching the end of the day now. [do not use: interviewer question]
[05:22.6] Any note of gratitude you would like to share with the Watsi community? [do not use: interviewer question]
